covers: INT 21h, the DOS services the pilot writes: file calls and IOCTL subfunctions.

rows.text: Create temporary file, a DOS 3.0 call: makes a file with a unique name.
CX holds the attribute of the new file.
DS:DX points to an ASCIZ path ending in a backslash, with room for 13 more bytes.
On success CF is clear, AX holds a read/write handle and DS:DX the path with the generated name added.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 03h, 04h or 05h.
The name is unique and the file must be deleted explicitly.
MS-DOS 3.0 to 4.0 name the file in hex digits from the date and time; MS-DOS 6 and later use letters A to P.
MS-DOS 5.0 inserts a missing trailing backslash, so an empty path makes a file in the root.
MS-DOS 5.00 revisions A and B and PC-DOS 5.00 revision A hang when the root directory is full.
MS-DOS 6.2x hangs when the path holds two consecutive separators.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x5a.
CX is never passed on: the file is always created with attribute 0.
The name is eight random letters A to Z in every DOS version, never hex digits.
A failing create returns false at once with the error code set; nothing here loops on it.
The path is handed to the create as it was read from DS:DX.
The error code is cleared before the create and restored on success.
Create or truncate a file, a DOS 2 call (CREAT).
CX holds the attributes of the new file.
Bit 0 read-only, 1 hidden, 2 system, 5 archive, 7 shareable under NetWare; bit 3, volume label, is ignored.
Bit 4 (directory) is reserved and must be zero.
DS:DX points to an ASCIZ filename.
On success CF is clear and AX holds the file handle.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 03h, 04h or 05h.
A file that already exists is truncated to zero length.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x3c.
AX is the DOS error code left behind, which can also be 02h file not found.
A name that is a device is opened for reading instead of created.
A name that cannot be made into a full path fails with the error DOS_MakeName set.
Trailing dots and spaces of the full name are removed first.
A free slot of the file table is searched for; a full table fails with 04h.
The handle comes from the process's own table, and a full one fails with 04h.
A failed create by the drive that is not access denied or write protected is 03h or 02h.
The call forces short names and may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay.
Open an existing file, a DOS 2 call (OPEN).
AL holds the access and sharing modes.
DS:DX points to an ASCIZ filename.
CL is an attribute mask of the files to look for, in a server call only.
On success CF is clear and AX holds the file handle.
On error CF is set and AX holds 01h, 02h, 03h, 04h, 05h, 0Ch or 56h.
The file pointer is set to the start of the file.
If SHARE or a network is loaded the open may fail because the file is already open, by the sharing modes.
Handles inherited from a parent also inherit its sharing and access restrictions.
Files with the hidden or system attribute may be opened.
Sharing modes work on local drives only if SHARE is loaded.
Bits 2-0 select the access mode: 0 read only, 1 write only, 2 read/write.
From DOS 5, value 3 is internal: it is passed to the redirector on EXEC for case-sensitive names.
Bit 3 is reserved and zero.
From DOS 3.0 bits 6-4 select the sharing mode: 0 compatibility, 1 deny all, 2 deny write, 3 deny read, 4 deny none.
Sharing mode 7 is the network FCB, only during a server call.
Bit 7 set makes the file private to the process and not inherited by children.
In DOS 2 to 6.22 a second open succeeds, fails with 05h or raises INT 24, by the first and second sharing modes.
In DOS 7.x the table adds a reading-without-time-update access, and its outcomes differ from DOS 6.22.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x3d.
A directory or volume-label name fails with 05h access denied.
A failed open of a file that exists gives 05h when the mode is not read only; no other sharing conflict is tested here.
With the share option on, a failed open of an existing file on a local directory drive also gives 05h.
The open applies no sharing table of its own and raises no INT 24.
The open applies no DOS 7.x sharing table of its own.
Value 3 of the access mode has no special handling and no redirector is called.
On a DOS-V Japanese display, with the input-method flags set, $IBMAIAS and MS$KANJI return their own handles, as does $IBMAFNT; on a PC-98 so does AVSDRV$$.
A name that is a device opens that device instead of a file.
A free slot of the file table is searched for; a full table fails with 04h.
The handle comes from the process's own table, and a full one fails with 04h.
A drive that fails with 0Ch access code invalid ends the open with that code; the error code is restored.
The open records no restriction of its own for a child to inherit; AL goes to the drive as given.
A name that cannot be made into a full path fails with the error DOS_MakeName set.
A failed open of a file that exists but is write-protected is 05h, else 03h or 02h.
If the open fails and long names are on, it is tried again with the original mode.
The call forces short names for the first try and may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay.
Close a file, a DOS 2 call (CLOSE).
BX holds the file handle.
On success CF is clear and AX is destroyed.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 06h.
A file that was written gets its pending writes done, its time and date stamps set to now and its directory entry updated.
Recent versions of DOS preserve AH, because some versions of Multiplan depended on it.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x3e.
The closing handle of $IBMAIAS, MS$KANJI, $IBMAFNT or AVSDRV$$ clears its device handle and succeeds.
The file's drive is read before the close, for the disk delay.
The call may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay.
A handle beyond the table or with no open file fails with 06h.
The close ends when the last reference goes; console, aux and printer stay in the table.
AL returns the reference count the file had before the close, plus nothing else.
Read from a file or device, a DOS 2 call (READ).
BX holds the file handle.
CX holds the number of bytes to read.
DS:DX points to the buffer for the data.
On success CF is clear and AX holds the bytes actually read, 0 at end of file before the call.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 05h or 06h.
Data is read from the current file position, which is updated after a successful read.
AX may be smaller than the request in CX when a partial read happened.
Reading from CON stops at the first CR.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x3f.
The call may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay.
A read that passes the end of the 64 KB segment with DX not a multiple of 16 is cut to 64 KB minus DX modulo 16.
An invalid or closed handle sets error 06h.
A handle of an external device reads through the device driver's read function.
A read that fails with error 77 runs the break action and may leave the call without an answer.
The echo flag is set during the read for the console.
A delay for the disk follows a read, except on a network resource.
Write to a file or device, a DOS 2 call (WRITE).
BX holds the file handle.
CX holds the number of bytes to write.
DS:DX points to the data to write.
On success CF is clear and AX holds the number of bytes actually written.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 05h or 06h.
With CX zero nothing is written and the file is truncated or extended to the current position.
Data is written at the current file position, which is updated after a successful write.
On FAT32 a file must be opened with AX=6C00h and the extended size flag to grow past 2 GB, else the write fails with 05h.
AX below CX on return is usually caused by a full disk.
In DOS 5.0 to 6.0 a zero-byte write that extends the file seems to succeed even when the disk is too full.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x40.
The call never checks an extended size flag: it passes the write on as it is.
The result of a zero-byte write comes straight from the drive and is returned as is.
The call may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay.
A write that passes the end of the 64 KB segment, with DX not a multiple of 16, is cut to 64 KB minus DX modulo 16.
A write to handle 2 of the text Packed file is corrupt is detected and may be dropped, by the autofix settings.
An invalid or closed handle sets error 06h.
A handle of an external device writes through the device driver's write function.
A delay for the disk follows a write.
A write while the guest OS is running ends the emulator with an error.
Delete a file, a DOS 2 call (UNLINK).
DS:DX points to an ASCIZ filename, with no wildcards but see the notes.
CL is the attribute mask for deletion, in a server call only.
On success CF is clear; AX is destroyed in DOS 3.3 and AL seems to be the drive of the deleted file.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 02h, 03h or 05h.
From DOS 3.1 wildcards are allowed through AX=5D00h with a canonical filespec, and only files matching the mask in CL are deleted.
DOS does not erase the file's data; the file only becomes inaccessible because its FAT chain is cleared.
Deleting an open file may corrupt the filesystem; unless SHARE is loaded DOS does not close its handles.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x41.
A failed delete can also return 13h write protected, which the drive left.
The call sets short-name mode, and the find-loop delete for wildcard names is taken only when that mode is off.
The call forces short names, may unmask IRQ 0, and delays for the disk after a successful delete.
A device name fails with 05h access denied.
A name that cannot be made into a full path fails with the error DOS_MakeName set.
A read-only file cannot be deleted: the delete fails with 05h, unless the name has wildcards.
The drive's own delete decides the result; AL is set to the drive number on success.
With long names on and not forced short, a wildcard name deletes every match found by a find loop, skipping directories.
Set the current file position, a DOS 2 call (LSEEK).
AL is the origin of the move: 00h start of file, 01h current position, 02h end of file.
BX holds the file handle.
CX:DX is the signed offset from the origin.
On success CF is clear and DX:AX holds the new position in bytes from the start.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h or 06h.
For origins 01h and 02h the position may go before the start of the file with no error; later I/O then fails.
A position beyond the end of file extends it on the next write; on FAT32 a file needs the extended size flag past 2 GB.
In some versions of DOS, seeking to grow a file from zero to a large size can corrupt the FAT.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x42.
The result of the seek comes from the file's own seek; nothing in the call can corrupt the FAT.
The call may unmask IRQ 0 for the disk delay, which follows a successful seek.
An invalid or closed handle sets error 06h.
Terminate with a return code, a DOS 2 call (EXIT).
AL holds the return code.
The call never returns.
Unless the process is its own parent, all its open files are closed.
Unless the process is its own parent, all the memory belonging to it is freed.
All network file locks should be removed before the call.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x4c.
The return code and the termination type, exit or TSR, are stored for AH=4Dh.
The AMIS UTF-8 providers are told the process ended.
The directory search snapshots of the process are closed with its files.
The parent PSP becomes current and its saved registers and stack are restored, with INT 22's address as the return point.
The process name is updated and the error code cleared.
If the CPU core or cycles were set automatically by the program they are put back, and the title updated.
A termination inside the INT 23h break handling throws an internal exit.
The call leaves AX at 3E01h, as a program that needs a nonzero AL expects.
Find the first matching file, a DOS 2 call (FINDFIRST).
AL is a special flag for APPEND, used after INT 2F AX=B711h.
CX is the file attribute mask; bits 0 and 5 are ignored.
DS:DX points to an ASCIZ file specification that may hold a path and wildcards.
On success CF is clear and the DTA is filled with a FindFirst data block.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 02h, 03h or 12h.
For attributes other than 08h, files with at most the given mix of hidden, system and directory attributes are returned.
In DOS 2.x searching for attribute 08h, volume label, also returns normal files.
In DOS 3.0 and later searching for attribute 08h returns only the volume label, if any.
The call also succeeds for the name of a character device without wildcards.
DOS 2.x returns, for a device name, attribute 00h, size 0 and the current date and time.
DOS 3.0 and later return attribute 40h and the current date and time for a device name.
After INT 2F AX=B711h the name at DS:DX is overwritten with the found path, or prepended to the filespec when AL is not 0.
Under DOS 3.x and 4.x a second search for a device name with the volume-label bit fails without an intervening search.
In PC-DOS 3.10 and 4.01 and MS-DOS 3.2, 3.3 and 5.0 the block holds the drive at 00h, the 11-byte template at 01h and the attributes at 0Ch.
In DOS 2.x the block holds the attributes at 00h, the drive at 01h and the 11-byte template at 02h.
In DOS 2.x and most 3.x the block holds an entry count at 0Dh, a pointer to the DTA at 0Fh and a cluster number at 13h.
In PC-DOS 4.01 and MS-DOS 3.2, 3.3 and 5.0 the block holds an entry count at 0Dh, a cluster number at 0Fh and 4 reserved bytes at 11h.
In all versions the block holds at 15h the attribute, 16h the time, 18h the date, 1Ah the size and 1Eh the ASCIZ name.
AL is never read: the call keeps no APPEND flag.
The name at DS:DX is only read: it is never overwritten with a found path.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x4e.
A search for exactly attribute 08h, except on a CD-ROM, goes down the volume-label path whatever the version.
The test for exactly attribute 08h comes before the device check, so such a search with a device name is a label search.
The date and time of a device name are left at zero, with a note to use the current ones.
A device name returns attribute 40h with size, date and time all zero, not the current time.
The block follows one layout whatever the version: the 3.2 and 5.0 one with a drive number from 1 at 00h.
At 0Dh is a directory search ID and at 0Fh a 32-bit cluster number, for several searches at once.
At 0Dh is a directory search ID and at 0Fh a 32-bit cluster number, with 2 filler bytes at 13h.
The path is checked part by part before the search when long names are off, and a bad part gives 03h or 12h.
A volume search takes an optional drive, the label is the root's, and a name of dots or a missing directory fails.
The search is split into a directory and a pattern; a trailing backslash fails with 12h, and CD-ROM names are special.
An FCB search of the CHKDSK program drops the directory attribute; the drive, DTA and device name are set up.
The search is remembered for FindNext in a snapshot, with the drive and a wildcard flag.
The long-name search handles and their drive, attribute and name arrays are set before the DTA fields.
On success AX is set to zero, which the source marks undocumented.
A path error found beforehand, when long names are off, is set and returned.
The long-name find handle is cleared first.
The result keeps long and short names too, and the name is padded with spaces to 8 bytes.
IOCTL get device information, a DOS 2 call.
BX holds the handle.
On success CF is clear, DX holds the device information word and AX is destroyed.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h, 05h or 06h.
For a character device DH is the high byte of the driver's attribute word.
Character device: bit 14 the driver takes IOCTL, 13 output until busy, 11 OPEN and CLOSE; bit 7 set, 6 EOF on input, 5 raw, 4 special via INT 29.
For a character device bit 3 is a clock device, 2 the NUL device, 1 standard output and 0 standard input.
Bit 8 is unknown and is set by the MS-DOS 6.2x KEYB.
For a disk file bit 15 is remote and 14 skips the date and time on close, from DOS 3.0; bit 11 is media not removable.
For a disk file bit 8, DOS 4 only, raises INT 24 on a full disk or a read past the end.
For a disk file bit 7 is clear, bit 6 means not written, and bits 5-0 hold the drive number, 0 for A:.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x44 and DOS_IOCTL by its case 0x00.
For a device the call returns the device's own information word, with a character-device bit added.
For a device the call returns the device's own information word, not computed bits.
For a device bit 8 is whatever the device's own information word holds.
For a file the bits above 4 are the file object's own, not computed here.
For a file bit 8 is the file object's own: no INT 24 is raised by this call.
A file whose drive is unknown reports C: as its drive.
The DOS-V device handles IAS and MS$KANJI are answered first: both give DX=0080h for 00h; MS$KANJI also answers 02h with CX=4 and fails any other call with AX=1.
IOCTL set device information, a DOS 2 call.
BX holds the handle, which must refer to a character device.
DX holds the device information word; DH must be zero for DOS versions before 6.x.
On success CF is clear.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h, 05h, 06h or 0Dh.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x44 and DOS_IOCTL by its case 0x01.
A DH other than zero fails with 0Dh data invalid in every DOS version.
The call sets the device's information word and returns the word's low byte in AL.
IOCTL get input status, a DOS 2 call.
BX holds the file handle.
On success AL is 00h when not ready, for a device, or at end of file, for a file, and FFh when ready.
AH may be destroyed.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h, 05h, 06h or 0Dh.
Files may not register as at end of file if they were positioned there by AH=42h.
Under DOS 5.0, on success, AH holds the next character to be read, or 1Ah at end of file.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x44 and DOS_IOCTL by its case 0x06.
A file at its end by AH=42h also reads as at end: the call compares the current position with the end.
AH is never set to the next character or to 1Ah: only AL changes.
For a file the call seeks to the end to measure, then restores the position.
IOCTL get output status, a DOS 2 call.
BX holds the file handle.
On success AL is 00h when not ready and FFh when ready.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h, 05h, 06h or 0Dh.
From DOS 2 files are always ready for output, even with a full disk or no media in the drive.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x44 and DOS_IOCTL by its case 0x07.
A handle of an external device asks the device for its output status and returns it in AL.
IOCTL check if a block device is removable, a DOS 3.0 call.
BL is the drive number: 00h for the default, 01h for A:, and so on.
On success CF is clear and AX is the media type: 0000h removable, 0001h fixed.
On error CF is set and AX holds the error code 01h or 0Fh.
The INT 21h handler reaches it by its case 0x44 and DOS_IOCTL by its case 0x08.
A removable drive that is not A: or B:, such as a CD-ROM, fails with 01h instead of answering 0000h.
Drives A: and B: answer removable when they exist and fail with 0Fh when not; any other drive that is not removable answers fixed.
